The research team used a small electronic capsule that participants swallowed to monitor changes as it passed through the digestive system.

A scientific study carried out by the University of Copenhagen has found that drinking coffee regularly may affect the functioning of the digestive system, especially bowel movements and colon contractions and is also linked to greater diversity of gut bacteria.

The study was published in the journal "Gut Microbiology", which specialises in research on gut microorganisms, and aimed to explore the relationship between habitual coffee consumption and the physiological conditions inside the digestive system.

What does coffee do inside your digestive system?

The research team used a small electronic capsule that participants swallowed to track the changes that occurred as it travelled through the digestive system.

The capsule measured a set of indicators, including the time it took contents to pass through the gastrointestinal tract, temperature, acidity levels and intestinal contractions.

The study involved 61 healthy adults in Denmark, whom the researchers divided into two groups according to how much coffee they consumed.

The first group consisted of people who drank between one and five cups of coffee a day on more than three of the eight days covered by the study, while the second group comprised people who drank coffee less frequently.

The results showed that people who consume coffee regularly have greater diversity in the microorganisms present in their intestines compared with participants who drink less coffee.

This finding is consistent with research suggesting that coffee may influence the composition of the gut microbiome, the community of bacteria and other microorganisms that live inside the digestive system.

Francesca Bucci, the lead researcher in the study and a PhD student in the Department of Nutrition, Exercise and Sports at the University of Copenhagen, said that regular coffee consumption seems to affect the physiology of the intestines.

One of the most notable results was that people who drink coffee regularly had much lower acidity levels in the small intestine than those who consume it less often.

The researchers also observed a link between higher coffee intake and a greater number of contractions in the colon, muscle movements that help push intestinal contents through the digestive system.

These contractions play a role in digestion and in keeping bowel movements regular, as they help move waste along and may help prevent constipation and keep the intestinal muscles in good condition.

Bucci said that intestinal contractions can support proper digestion, help reduce constipation and help maintain the functional state of the intestinal muscles.

By contrast, the researchers are still unable to determine whether the lower level of acidity in the small intestine benefits health or could have negative effects.

Is coffee responsible for the changes?

The researchers stress that the study cannot prove that coffee consumption is the direct cause of the changes observed in the digestive system.

However, Henrik Munch Roager, associate professor and head of the research group in the Department of Nutrition, Exercise and Sports at the University of Copenhagen, believes there are reasons to support the possibility that coffee plays a role in these changes.

He explained that previous studies have shown that coffee affects a range of processes that take place inside the digestive system, including the secretion of acids in the stomach.

He added that this evidence makes it likely that the differences the researchers observed are linked to the effects of coffee rather than being mere coincidence.

He pointed out that many people notice, based on their daily experience, that coffee affects their digestion.

The research team sees the next step as conducting a study that allows control over the amount of coffee participants drink, instead of merely observing their consumption habits and comparing the differences between them.

This type of study would help determine whether coffee is actually causing these changes and to understand the mechanisms through which it may affect bowel movements and contractions.

Concret, “prin această decizie, care epuizează ultima cale extraordinară de atac prevăzută de Convenția ICSID, hotărârea arbitrală prin care au fost respinse integral pretențiile de aproximativ 6,5 miliarde de dolari formulate împotriva României rămâne definitivă și obligatorie. Instituția detaliază că suma pretinsă reprezintă echivalentul a aproximativ 31,5 miliarde lei, respectiv circa 1,5% din PIB-ul brut al României în acest an.

Canadian authorities said Russians will be barred from the 10-nation tournament in Alberta from 26 December. Estonia, Finland and Norway plan to exclude athletes until the war in Ukraine ends.

The Russian Ice Hockey Federation is insisting that the World Junior Championship, due to take place in Canada next month, be postponed or cancelled after Ottawa decided not to allow the Russian team to take part in the tournament.

As the official Russian news agency TASS reported on Thursday, the president of the Russian Ice Hockey Federation, Vladislav Tretiak, threatened to demand compensation from Canada and possibly also from Germany, which will host the men’s World Championship in 2027, if Russia is barred from participation.

Speaking at a meeting of the Presidential Council for the Development of Physical Culture and Sport in Moscow, Tretiak said he had also appealed to the International Ice Hockey Federation’s (IIHF) ethics committee to open an investigation and impose sanctions on national federations that are organising boycotts of games involving Russia.

"There are rules: if a team does not take to the ice, it suffers a technical defeat and sanctions are imposed," TASS quoted Tretiak as saying. "The IIHF has a way out - either they let us play, or, if we are unable to enter Canada, they move the championship, do not stage it at all, or impose sanctions on the Canadian ice hockey association."

"You cannot bomb Ukrainian cities and then send your juniors... as if you were civilised people"

Tretiak’s statement came a day after Canada confirmed that Russian players would not be allowed to compete in the 10-nation tournament, which is due to begin on 26 December in the province of Alberta. Canada adopted this stance in response to a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) last month that restored Russia’s right to take part in international ice hockey competitions.

That decision overturned the ban the IIHF had imposed on Russia after the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"You cannot bomb Ukrainian cities and then send your juniors to Alberta to play hockey, as if you were civilised people. No Russian or Belarusian teams at the World Junior Championship. Not under your flags. Not under any other flags. Period," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in an unequivocal statement.

As the Russian sports daily Sport-Express reported (source in Russian), Russia had from the outset expected that visas for the World Championship would be refused, so the Russian Ice Hockey Federation was planning to put together a squad made up solely of players from North American NHL clubs. However, Ottawa said that even these Russians would not be able to play for the national team in any case because their work visas do not allow it.

In addition, Germany and several other countries have refused to sign the new schedule for the World Junior Championship if Russia is included. The head of the German Ice Hockey Association, Frank Lutz, said this at a meeting of the Bundestag’s sports committee (link in German) (source in Russian).

The next tournament in the ice hockey calendar is the women’s under-18 World Championship in Ostrava, Czechia, from 8 to 16 January 2027, but Prague has also made it clear in advance that it will not issue visas to Russian players.

For its part, Germany is considering dropping the men’s World Championship in spring 2027 against the background of a wave of boycotts. Several of the world’s leading ice hockey nations have said they will not play Russia after the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled that Russia and Belarus should be readmitted to international ice hockey competitions.

Meanwhile, Germany’s "fringe" parties, the far-right Alternative for Germany and the far-left Die Linke, have called (source in Russian) (link in German) on Berlin not to obstruct the participation of the Russian team.

The International Ice Hockey Federation is so far refraining from commenting on the dispute, finding itself at the centre of a rapidly escalating conflict. A number of national federations, including those of Canada, Sweden, Finland, Germany, Czechia and Latvia, have already announced that they will not play matches against Russia. Some tournament sponsors have also threatened to end their cooperation if Russia is allowed to take part.

For the IIHF, moving the World Junior Championship at such a late stage would be extremely difficult; it would also be very hard to find another country willing to take over as host from Canada. On Sunday Norway said it had received notification from the IIHF that it was being excluded from the tournament, to make room for Russia. The federation itself has not yet announced this change.

Several northern countries plan to bar all Russian athletes

Finland is tightening (source in Russian) (link in English) restrictions on the entry of Russian citizens into the country. On 12 November 2026 the government adopted a decree stating that the entry of Russian citizens poses a threat to Finland’s international relations. The new restrictions cover short-term work carried out on the basis of a visa, including professional sport.

"As long as Russia’s aggressive war continues, Russian athletes have no business in Finland. Their entry into the country would pose a threat to Finland’s international relations. The same applies to other types of short-term work on visas that do not serve Finland’s vital national interests," said Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen.

The restrictions will apply to all Russian athletes, including those competing under neutral status. The Foreign Ministry said Russia "uses sport as a propaganda tool and seeks to exploit it to advance the aims of its illegal war of aggression".

Oslo has announced similar steps following Helsinki’s decision. The Norwegian government intends to expel Russian and Belarusian professional athletes and their entourages if they try to enter the country to take part in sporting events while the war in Ukraine continues.

The Norwegian government statement stresses that Russian elite sport is closely linked to the authorities and therefore cannot be "considered in isolation" from the war in Ukraine. Belarus, it notes, has supported and facilitated Russia’s war, according to the text (link in Norwegian) (source in Russian).

"Since Russia continues its brutal war of aggression, the government does not want Russian and Belarusian professional athletes and their support staff to come to Norway to take part in international sporting events," said Minister of Culture and Equality Lubna Boby Jaffery.

The government decision, which will come into force "in the near future", could affect the participation of Moscow and Minsk in several events, in particular the opening round of the FIS Ski Jumping World Cup in Lillehammer from 20 to 22 November.

Finally, the authorities in Tallinn have notified the International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS) that athletes from Russia and Belarus will not be able to take part in competitions held in Estonia. From 18 to 24 January, Otepää will host the World Championships for juniors and under-23 athletes in Nordic skiing, and in February the World Biathlon Championships will take place at the Tehvandi Sports Centre ski stadium.

"Estonia has firmly condemned Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine from the very beginning. Since then, the Estonian government, the Ministry of Culture and the Estonian Olympic Committee have held to a common position that Russian and Belarusian athletes and teams must not take part in international sports competitions until the war in Ukraine is over," says a letter from the Ministry of Culture to FIS, the details of which have been reported (source in Russian) in the press.

At the same time, there were reports that Russia has refused (source in Russian) to take part in the European Boxing Championships for athletes aged 19 to 22, which will be held from 15 to 24 November in Porec, Croatia. The reasons were the Croatian authorities’ requirement that they compete without the Russian flag and anthem, and the refusal to issue visas to members of the Russian delegation.

MEPs want public bodies to buy more European cloud services. The continent’s alternatives are growing, but they remain a fraction of the size of Amazon, Microsoft and Google.

Microsoft Outlook and Teams users around the world, including in Europe, were locked out of their emails and meetings this week after a global outage. The disruption has renewed questions about how much the continent relies on a few American firms.

“The episode shows once again the downside of depending so heavily on a handful of large US tech companies,” Tommaso Valletti told Euronews Next.

Valletti is Professor of Economics at Imperial College Business School in London, United Kingdom, and was the European Commission’s chief competition economist from 2016 to 2019.

The disruption began on Thursday afternoon European time and hit users in 74 countries and territories, according to the outage tracker Downdetector. In the UK, some doctors' surgeries told patients to phone them with urgent queries.

Microsoft said there was no sign of a cyber attack but has not yet named a root cause. Services were still being gradually restored on Friday. It follows Microsoft 365 outages in January and August.

How dependent is Europe?

Amazon, Microsoft and Google together hold about 70% of the European cloud market, according to Synergy Research Group. European providers account for around 15%, down from about 29% in 2017. The largest of them, Germany’s SAP and Deutsche Telekom, hold just 2% each.

Euronews has previously reported that around 80% of Europe’s digital infrastructure and technology comes from outside the EU.

That sits uneasily with the public. Most EU citizens want European-controlled digital infrastructure, according to the latest Eurobarometer survey. Support is highest in Sweden (94%), Finland (93%) and Denmark (92%).

Brussels wants Europe to buy European

On Wednesday, MEPs presented their draft report on the Commission’s proposed Cloud and AI Development Act. The report calls for public authorities to buy more cloud services from European providers.

“Our critical systems run on someone else’s technology, and someone else can switch it off,” warned Dutch Green MEP Reinier van Lanschot.

Fears of a so-called “kill switch” grew in June, when Anthropic suspended access to its Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 AI models to comply with US export controls. Access was restored on 1 July.

The Commission also wants to triple the EU’s data centre capacity within five to seven years. Bidding for up to seven EU-backed AI “gigafactories” closed on Thursday.

Who could take on the giants?

Europe has no single rival to Microsoft, Amazon or Google. Instead, it has contenders at different layers of the technology stack.

France’s Mistral AI is Europe’s best-known maker of AI models. It was valued at €21 billion after a €3 billion funding round led by Samsung in September.

In cloud computing, STACKIT, owned by the Lidl and Kaufland parent company Schwarz Group, is building an €11 billion AI data centre in Brandenburg, Germany. In April, STACKIT and France’s OVHcloud, Scaleway and Mistral were among the firms that won places on the Commission’s own sovereign cloud contract, worth up to €180 million.

In hardware, Germany’s Infineon is a leading maker of the power chips that run AI data centres. Analysts at this week’s SEMICON Europa trade fair in Munich, Germany, identified power chips as Europe’s strongest way into the AI boom.

Will Europeans switch?

Willingness to pay more for an EU-based provider varies widely. Danes (76%), Swedes and Croatians (both 73%) are the most willing, while Estonians (35%), Bulgarians and Czechs (both 45%) are the least, according to Eurobarometer.

Businesses are cautious too. In a survey by the German digital association Bitkom, 85% of German companies said the country was too dependent on US cloud providers, yet 71% use one. Research firm IDC found that only 4% of European organisations plan to use local providers exclusively.

US firms are also adapting. Amazon Web Services launched its European Sovereign Cloud in Brandenburg in January, run by a separate EU-based company.

Synergy’s chief analyst, John Dinsdale, has told CNBC that European providers will struggle to reverse their loss of market share.

What happens next?

Parliament committees will discuss the proposed Cloud and AI Development Act draft report on 1 December. A committee vote is provisionally scheduled for mid-March 2027, followed by a plenary vote in April.

Microsoft has said it will publish a report on the cause of the outage once services are fully restored.

US Transport Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the stoppage on what he called an "incredibly old" air traffic control system and warned that it would take time for normal operations to resume.

Passengers travelling to and from the United States continue to face delays and cancellations to flights on Saturday morning despite the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) having lifted a nationwide ground stop.

The rare order had been issued on Friday following a "telecommunications outage," with all flights halted across the country.

The FAA has since lifted the ground stop and said that some flight departures were resuming.

"Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable," the agency said, while advising travellers to contact airlines for flight updates.

US Transport Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the stoppage on what he called an "incredibly old" air traffic control system and warned that it would take time for normal operations to resume.

"At 8:15 (pm) tonight, eastern time, we've opened up the airspace. Now does that mean every flight is going to fly? Right now, it's going to be slow," he told reporters. "It depends on do we have crews available, do we have pilots and flight attendants available to fly your flight. We're going to try to move as many of those as we can tonight."

"But it's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened," he added.

Flight-tracking site Flightradar24's airport disruption map shows major problems at airports across the US on Saturday morning.

FlightAware, another tracking service, put the number of cancellations to flights to or from the US on Friday at more than 8,860. It said around 2,650 more have been cancelled so far on Saturday.

United Airlines, Delta and American have all said they are resuming flight operations.

"We're focused on operating as many remaining flights as possible this evening while positioning the airline for the strongest possible recovery in the days ahead," American said in a statement late on Friday.

Teachers and health workers are among the hardest to recruit in the EU, according to the OECD. Experts explain why some jobs are harder to fill than others.

Teaching, healthcare and IT jobs are among the hardest to fill across Europe, while employers generally find it easier to recruit labourers and food preparation assistants. But the pattern varies by country. Spain, for example, faces a large shortage of food preparation assistants, according to the OECD.

These shortages persist even as young people face a tougher job market. The OECD found that the unemployment gap between young graduates and the wider working-age population has widened in the countries it analysed. The European Central Bank (ECB) also found that job prospects for young people in the eurozone have weakened since 2023.

Among the EU countries covered by the OECD’s Mapping Skill Shortages in OECD Countries report, teaching ranks as the hardest occupation to fill on average, followed by health professionals and information and communications technology (ICT) professionals. Health associate professionals, such as medical technicians and some nursing staff, and business and administration professionals complete the top five.

At the other end, labourers are the easiest to recruit, followed by elementary workers, food preparation assistants, sales workers and assemblers.

The OECD’s index compares occupations within each country. Positive scores point to relative shortages and negative scores to relative surpluses. The scores show how hard jobs are to fill compared with other occupations in the same country. They do not count vacancies or missing workers. The data are from 2024 for most countries.

The trends across 27 European countries, including Norway, Switzerland, Turkey and the UK, show which occupations most often appear among the five hardest or easiest to fill.

Top five occupations that are hardest to fill

Teachers are among the five hardest occupations to fill in 13 countries. Health professionals and ICT professionals follow, with 12 countries each. In seven countries, managers make the top five, while health associate professionals, personal care workers, and business and administration professionals each do so in six countries.

Top five occupations that are easiest to fill

Labourers are among the five easiest occupations to fill in 14 countries, followed by food preparation assistants in 12 and other clerical workers in 11. Elementary workers make the list in 10 countries and assemblers in eight.

Looking beyond the five highest and lowest scores, the OECD groups occupations into five categories, depending on how hard it is to fill them compared with other occupations in the same country. This shows that health, teaching and ICT jobs are hard to fill in most countries.

Why is Europe short of doctors and nurses?

Health professionals are hard to find in 23 of the 27 countries, while health associate professionals are in short supply in 21. Health associates are also hard to find in 21 countries.

“EU and European healthcare systems are unable to retain and recruit nurses at the frontline of care, which is leading to extensive nursing shortages everywhere,” Paul De Raeve and Manuel Ballotta of the European Federation of Nurses Associations (EFN) told Euronews Business.

They said high patient-to-nurse ratios, unsafe working conditions and widespread mental health problems make nursing less attractive. They also pointed to low pay, limited career prospects, a lack of professional recognition and frequent exposure to harassment and violence.

Dr Ole Johan Bakke, president of the Standing Committee of European Doctors (CPME), pointed to worsening working conditions.

“Doctors across Europe are increasingly expected to compensate for systemic workforce shortages through excessive working hours and increased workloads. Violence against healthcare professionals, an increasingly common phenomenon experienced by doctors, further compounds these problems,” he told Euronews Business.

He said these pressures contribute to burnout and make medicine less attractive as a lifelong career.

Teacher shortages go beyond pay

Teachers are hard to find in 21 countries. In the other six countries (Germany, Greece, Italy, Norway, Spain and Turkey), the OECD classifies teaching as broadly in balance.

“Teacher shortages are no longer simply a question of filling vacant positions; they increasingly concern the long-term attractiveness and sustainability of the teaching profession,” Daniel Wisniewski, secretary general of the European Federation of Education Employers, told Euronews Business.

He said competitive salaries remain essential, but teachers also face growing demands as schools adopt digital tools, make classrooms more inclusive and take on more responsibility for student wellbeing. Teachers also face more administrative work.

He pointed out that the reasons behind teacher shortages go well beyond pay, although competitive salaries remain an essential factor. Teaching has become an increasingly complex profession, with demands as schools adopt digital tools, make classrooms more inclusive and take on more responsibility for student wellbeing. Teachers also face more administrative work.

“We need to recognise that teachers' working conditions, professional autonomy, career development opportunities and the quality of school leadership are equally important in determining whether people enter and remain in the profession,” he said.

Will AI make ICT jobs easier to fill?

Information and communications technology (ICT) professionals and business and administration professionals are hard to find in 18 countries each. Isabel Skak Olufsen, an economist at the OECD, said digitalisation had increased demand for ICT professionals. However, advances in artificial intelligence (AI) may reduce demand for some ICT professionals in the future, particularly for entry-level positions, she added.

Low-skilled and routine jobs are the easiest to fill

Labourers are easy to find in 21 countries, followed by food preparation assistants in 17 and elementary workers in 16. Sales workers and other clerical workers are easy to find in 15 countries each.

Some countries go against the European pattern

In Norway, labourers are the hardest workers to recruit, even though they are relatively easy to find in 21 of the countries studied. Food preparation assistants are the hardest to recruit in Spain, although they are easy to find in much of Europe. In France, elementary workers are the hardest to recruit.

Several northern and western European countries buck the trend for ICT jobs. The OECD classifies the labour market for ICT professionals as broadly in balance in Denmark, Finland, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden, and in surplus in Austria, Switzerland and the UK.

Shortages depend on economic structure

“The occupations facing the greatest shortages differ across countries for several reasons. Demand for occupations depends on countries’ economic structure,” Olufsen told Euronews Business.

She pointed to South Korea and Germany, where large manufacturing sectors help explain shortages in several mid-skilled occupations, including assemblers and machine operators.

The supply of workers also varies by country, Olufsen said. Countries that pay teachers and health professionals relatively well may face fewer shortages in those occupations.

Skills matching and training

“Europe’s labour shortages are increasingly structural rather than temporary. Demographic change, skills mismatches, job quality and limited labour mobility all play a role,” Pia-Johanna Fallström, a spokesperson for the European Labour Authority (ELA), told Euronews Business.

She said Europe needs better training, jobs with better working conditions and a better match between workers’ skills and employers’ needs. She also called for fair labour mobility to help workers in countries with a surplus find jobs where they are needed.

“ELA’s analysis shows that many occupations reported as being in shortage in one country can be a surplus elsewhere,” she added.

Transitioning away from fossil fuels appears to have become an elephant in the room as the first week of COP31 wraps up.

Leaders are shying away from mentioning fossil fuels despite mounting warnings that the world will overshoot the 1.5℃ threshold, as the first week of COP31 discussions wraps up.

President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, addressed leaders in Antalya on Wednesday (11 November) – describing the recent bout of extreme weather and deadly wildfires that wrecked Europe and the rest of the world as the “summer of truth”.

“We are at a global tipping point,” she said. “The latest UN report is clear: We’re on course to overshoot the 1.5℃ target and every fraction of a degree matters.”

Von der Leyen laid out the EU’s priorities for COP31, including accelerating electrification and “strengthening global partnerships” to build clean economies – but at no point in her speech did she mention fossil fuels.

According to the UN, fossil fuels – coal, oil and gas – are by far the largest contributor to global climate change, accounting for around 68 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions and nearly 90 per cent of all carbon dioxide emissions.

Von der Leyen was accused of “missing the mark” by not mentioning a word on transitioning away from fossil fuels (TAFF) and for using a “celebratory tone” despite EU climate finance flatlining.

“Electrification needs to be clearly linked to a transition away from fossil fuels, otherwise it gives the fossil fuel industry cover to carry on as usual, raking in profits while ordinary people are hit by rising energy bills and impacts,” says Chiara Martinelli, Director at Climate Action Network (CAN) Europe.

Finland launches fossil fuel phaseout roadmap

Agreements at the UN summit require consensus from all parties – that’s nearly 200 nations – which means progress is often slow and incremental.

But that didn’t stop Finland from publishing a new domestic roadmap to TAFF at the event, following in the footsteps of France, Germany and the Netherlands.

After spearheading a global TAFF roadmap before handing over the COP presidency, Brazil is also actively working on its own domestic national roadmap, along with various Pacific Island Nations.

More than 96 per cent of Finland’s electricity is already generated from non-fossil sources, one of the highest shares in the world.

However, the energy intensity of the economy and energy consumption per capita are both very high due to the country’s relatively large heavy industry sector, long travel distances, and the high heating demand due to its cold climate.

In 2025 the largest individual energy source, wood fuels, accounted for 28 per cent of its total energy consumption, while nuclear and fossil fuels made up 27 and 18 per cent respectively.

The main domestic energy sources currently are wood-based fuels, hydropower, wind power, solar power, waste, peat, and heat pumps.

Finland, which aims to become carbon neutral by 2035, did not however set a legally binding deadline to TAFF. Its roadmap follows the Santa Marta process on TAFF after all mentions of establishing a fossil fuel transition roadmap were scrubbed from the final text of COP30 in Belém last year.

“It is positive to see more countries responding to the call to plan their future beyond fossil fuels,” says Romain Ioualalenof of non-profit Oil Change International.

“However, roadmaps need to be more than just a reiteration of existing policies: we need to see rich countries accelerate their exit from fossil fuels to align with global climate goals.”

Fossil fuel phaseout ‘doesn’t make sense’ without financing

Türkiye, France, the US and Italy are some of the countries that have brought fossil fuel lobbyists to the annual climate summit, once again drawing scrutiny of who gets a seat at the table and the integrity of its process.

Co-host Türkiye has also garnered criticism for its heavy reliance on coal, which remains its biggest source of power.

Despite pushing to expand renewables, the country’s national climate plan also allows for an increase in its greenhouse gas emissions rather than a decrease – as it continues to step up fossil fuel exploration both in the Black Sea and in the country’s south.

In fact, as COP31 kicked off on Monday (9 November), Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan celebrated the fact that the country had made an oil discovery on its territory.

On Thursday (12 November), Türkiye’s Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar – who has previously claimed that fossil fuels are required for energy security – said that developing countries need access to technology and financing or they won’t be able to make the transition to clean energy.

‘Without that, to tell the people you don’t need to consume coal, you don’t need to consume other fossil fuels, it doesn’t make any sense,’ he told news agency AFP.

“We need to produce this electricity. We would like to make it with renewables. We would like to make it with nuclear – but of course to develop nuclear power plants, a huge amount of finance [is] required.”

Financing is expected to become one of the most contested issues in Antalya, particularly to fund adaptation and loss and damage in countries most vulnerable to climate disasters, like developing nations and small island states.

At COP29 in Baku in 2024, developed countries agreed to mobilise at least $300 billion (€268bn) a year for developing nations by 2035, as part of a wider $1.3 trillion (€1.63tn) target from public and private sources.

At COP30 last year, governments agreed to push for at least a tripling of adaptation finance by 2035, but without settling the baseline, who pays or how the money will be delivered.

Analysts say one “feasible route to a meaningful outcome” on climate finance at COP31 would be anchoring the tripling pledge and agreeing a $40 billion (€36.2 billion) baseline with interim milestones before 2035 – with a minimum share of grants compared with loans.

But a UN Environment Programme (UNEP) report published days before the summit found that even tripling current international public adaptation finance would only meet 23-29 per cent of developing countries’ needs.

COP31’s electrification pledge gains momentum – and criticism

While TAFF is not on the official agenda for COP31, it has already become a flashpoint discussion due to the spiralling costs of oil and gas following the US-led war on Iran.

Fossil fuels have also become a growing concern given Türkiye’s 35-by-35 pledge. This would see the global share of energy demand met by electricity increase to 35 per cent, up from around 23 per cent today, by 2035.

More than a dozen countries and several small island states have publicly backed the goal, including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham – just weeks after his government approved the controversial Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.

Von der Leyen also showed support, arguing that the pledge is in reach and will provide greater energy security for the EU.

Electrification means replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels with electricity – such as going from a diesel-powered car to an electric vehicle (EV).

But critics warn that electrification in itself will not eradicate fossil fuel use and could be used as an excuse to allow governments to count expanded gas-fired generation as progress towards the 35-by-35 pledge.

“Switching from oil and gas to electricity only cuts emissions if that electricity is clean – making the rapid build-out of renewables non-negotiable,” says Linda Kalcher, executive director at pan-European think tank Strategic Perspectives

“Solar and wind are the cheapest and among the fastest sources of new electricity worldwide, even more since oil and gas prices soared. The risk of further fossil-fuel lock-in and investment in uneconomical oil and gas reserves remains though – not least as rising energy demand from data centres fuels calls for new fossil-fuel capacity.”

COP31 will end on 20 November.

From the French Alps to Austria’s historic mountain towns, these destinations offer everything from challenging ski runs to snowy walks, cosy restaurants and city sightseeing – with new and upgraded rail services making the journey easier.

The Alps offer plenty of reasons to visit in winter, even if you have no intention of putting on a pair of skis. Think pretty mountain villages, cosy restaurants, snowy walking trails and spectacular views.

Getting there is also becoming easier by train. For the 2026-2027 season, new direct rail links to Austria, upgraded sleeper services to Switzerland and the return of Eurostar Snow to the French Alps are opening up more ways to reach the mountains without flying.

For anyone keen to cut the carbon footprint of their winter escape, going by train is also a solid choice, as rail travel is far better for the environment than flying.

The experts at Rail Europe have picked out five Alpine destinations worth considering this winter, from resorts made for serious skiers to mountain retreats with plenty to offer those who prefer to keep their feet firmly on the ground.

The French Alps

The French Alps are a winter classic, whether you’re heading there to ski or simply fancy a few days in the mountains. Getting there is easier this season, too, with the return of Eurostar Snow and additional TGV services.

From 19 December, Eurostar Snow will connect Amsterdam, Schiphol Airport, Rotterdam, Antwerp and Brussels with six stations in the French Alps, including Moûtiers, Aime-la-Plagne and Bourg-Saint-Maurice.

There are also extra TGV INOUI services from France, with up to seven special trains running from Paris to Bourg-Saint-Maurice on peak days, as well as direct Saturday connections from northern France and services towards the Chamonix Valley.

Once there, Courchevel, La Plagne and Les Arcs are all within easy reach, and there's plenty to do beyond the slopes – from snowshoeing and winter walks to sledging, spa days and long lunches in mountain restaurants.

If you’re in Bourg-Saint-Maurice, try a seven-minute funicular ride which whisks visitors up to Arc 1600, a family-friendly, pedestrian-only village.

Innsbruck, Austria

If you’re keen to experience a city break with mountains on the doorstep, Innsbruck could be the place for you.

It’s going to be easier to get to the Austrian city next month, as a new daily direct ICE connection from Hanover, via Kassel and Würzburg, is set to launch on 13 December.

Innsbruck boasts a handsome medieval Old Town, traditional cafés and plenty of Tyrolean restaurants to explore. Be sure to visit the famous Golden Roof or, if you’re visiting from mid-November to the end of December, don’t miss the chance to wander around the city's Christmas markets.

An added bonus to this city is that the mountains are just minutes away. Its Nordkette cable cars, designed by Zaha Hadid, take visitors to around 2,300 metres in approximately 30 minutes.

Here, you’ll find steep, sun-soaked slopes – for all ability levels – as well as spectacular views across the city and the surrounding Austrian Alps.

St. Anton am Arlberg, Austria

St. Anton am Arlberg is one of Austria’s best-known winter resorts, drawing keen skiers with its challenging runs alongside a lively après-ski scene.

Getting there is set to be easier this season, with a seasonal ICE train connection from Frankfurt arriving on Saturdays and returning on Sundays from 13 December until 4 April.

The route continues along the scenic Arlberg railway to Landeck, opening up more of western Tyrol. Away from the slopes, visitors can explore winter walking trails, tuck into traditional Tyrolean food or spend an afternoon in one of the resort’s mountain bars.

Switzerland

Think of mountains, and you’ll probably think of Switzerland.

Getting there by train will soon become a more comfortable experience, thanks to upgraded Nightjet sleeper trains which will run from Amsterdam to Basel and Zurich, starting on 13 December.

Sleeping compartments and private mini compartments have been improved and make an excellent base for an overnight journey.

As well as exploring the delights of cities Basel or Zürich, travellers can also opt to continue towards the Swiss Alps by rail – and not an airport in sight.

Kitzbühel, Austria

Austria is seeing a particular boom in new routes this winter, and Kitzbühel is no exception.

The historic town may be best known for its famous Hahnenkamm ski race, but there’s plenty to enjoy here beyond the slopes.

Its medieval old town, with its colourful gabled houses, narrow cobblestone streets, and a 750-year history, is packed with traditional restaurants, cafés and shops, while winter walking routes offer a chance to take in the surrounding mountain scenery.

Getting there is more straightforward this season, too, with the seasonal ICE Großglockner set to run direct services from Hamburg and Hannover on selected weekends between 18 December 2026 and 4 April 2027.

Alerta a fost emisă la ora 15:54 (22:54 pe ora României), “din cauza unor circumstanțe extraordinare și din motive de siguranță”, a transmis Administrația Federală a Aviației din SUA (FAA). La momentul respectiv, agenția nu a oferit alte informații în afară de precizarea că “toate zborurile de plecare trebuie să rămână suspendate până la noi ordine”.

Restricția de decolare a fost ridicată la ora locală 20:15 (02:15 pe ora României). Conform platformei de monitorizare a zborurilor, FlightAware, interdicția a dus la peste 8.500 de zboruri întârziate și aproape 8.000 de zboruri anulate. 

Câteva ore mai târziu, secretarul Transporturilor, Sean Duffy, a atribuit întreruperea unui sistem de control al traficului aerian învechit, în care routerele “au fost supraîncărcate cu date”. Duffy a explicat, într-o conferință de presă la Casa Albă, că, odată ce routerele au devenit supraîncărcate, acest lucru a dus la “o instabilitate la nivelul radarelor și al comunicațiilor din centrele noastre, din TRACON-urile (centrul de control al traficului aerian – n.r.) noastre de pe întreg teritoriul țării”. Astfel, la nivelul centrului de control au fost observate inconsistențe în datele provenite de la radare și în comunicarea cu aeronavele, a spus Duffy. 

Secretarul Transporturilor a precizat că FAA nu și-a pierdut toate capacitățile de telecomunicații sau radar, dar, din cauza instabilității, s-a emis ordinul de oprire la sol ca măsură de precauție. La momentul interdicției zborurilor, se aflau peste 3.500 de avioane în aer, potrivit acestuia. 

Duffy a afirmat că problema imediată a fost rezolvată și că zborurile sunt sigure, dar a avertizat că este necesară o revizuire mai amplă a sistemului învechit de control al traficului aerian pentru a preveni defecțiuni similare. 

La rândul său, Secretarul Securității Interne, Markwayne Mullin, a declarat că, nu există dovezi care să sugereze un atac cibernetic în acest moment și că nu au fost semne de pericol pentru public. “FAA a reușit să gestioneze situația. Am luat această măsură preventiv”, a spus el într-o conferință de presă de la Casa Albă.

Potrivit firmei de date pentru industria aviației Cirium, aproximativ 1,5 milioane de persoane au rămas blocate din cauza anulărilor zborurilor.

O oprire generalizată a traficului aerian este o măsură extrem de rară în Statele Unite. După atacurile teroriste din 11 septembrie 2001, FAA a ordonat suspendarea tuturor zborurilor la nivel național. În ianuarie 2023, FAA a suspendat toate zborurile pentru câteva ore, invocând o defecțiune a sistemului “Notice to Air Missions”, care avertizează piloții cu privire la o serie de potențiale pericole. Astfel, incidentul de vineri reprezintă a doua interdicție de această amploare de la atentatele din 2001.
